summary: Peoplestown's long-neglected Four Corners Park is getting a $9.4 million makeover after the Bezos Earth Fund handed Park Pride the largest grant in its history. In Reynoldstown, a new duplex project called Gemini breaks ground on a former church corner a block off the BeltLine. Decatur WatchFest has drawn 140,000 people to the Square with 10 days of World Cup left, and Lionel Messi grabbed the tournament's Golden Boot lead with his eighth goal in Atlanta. The Atlanta History Center opens its most ambitious exhibit ever for its 100th birthday, a Grant Park mural honoring the late Jovita Moore is finally getting repainted, and Barnes & Noble returns to East Atlanta four years after leaving. Plus a Midtown steakhouse closes without warning and a runner dressed as a hot dog becomes a Peachtree Road Race legend.

topStory.headline: Bezos Earth Fund Gives $9.4 Million to Remake Peoplestown's Four Corners Park
topStory.summary: Park Pride's largest project ever will overhaul the long-neglected park that residents fought for decades to save, funded by the biggest grant in the nonprofit's history.
topStory.body: For the folks who have spent decades fighting for Peoplestown, this one lands different. Columbus Ward, the neighborhood elder some call its unofficial mayor, remembers playing softball on the vacant lot that eventually became Four Corners Park. He also remembers joining the fight to keep it from being demolished. For years, Ward and his neighbors pushed for the resources to make the little park what it could be. Now the money is here, and it is not a small amount. The Bezos Earth Fund is giving $9.4 million to Park Pride, the Atlanta nonprofit that builds and improves neighborhood parks, to completely rework Four Corners. Park Pride calls it the largest project in its history. That scale matters in a neighborhood that has watched a lot of investment flow to other parts of intown Atlanta while its own green space sat neglected. Peoplestown sits just south of the stadium district and has spent years pushing back on flooding, displacement, and broken promises. A nearly ten million dollar park redesign, driven by the people who live there, is the kind of win that does not come around often. Park Pride says it will work directly with Peoplestown residents on the design rather than dropping a plan on them. Given how hard this community fought to keep the park at all, that collaboration is the whole point.
topStory.imageAlt: Four Corners Park announcement in Peoplestown with Park Pride and Bezos Earth Fund

stories.headline: Decatur WatchFest Hits 140,000 Visitors With 10 Days of World Cup Left
stories.summary: The free viewing party on Decatur Square has become one of metro Atlanta's biggest World Cup gathering spots, with quarterfinals, the final, and seven concerts still to come.
stories.body: Turns out you did not need a Mercedes-Benz Stadium ticket to feel the World Cup this summer. You needed a lawn chair and a spot on Decatur Square. Decatur WatchFest has pulled in roughly 140,000 people over its first month, and the city says the biggest stretch is still ahead. For the next 10 days, three giant screens on the Square will carry the World Cup quarterfinals, semifinals, the third-place playoff, and the final. Watching is completely free and no ticket is required. The festival is not just soccer. Organizers have booked seven concerts to run alongside the matches, including a set from the Indigo Girls, the Decatur-rooted folk duo. If the Square fills up or a specific game is not on the big screens, the city has lined up official backup viewing spots nearby. For a small city that leans hard into its downtown, drawing six figures of visitors to a free public event is exactly the kind of thing Decatur likes to be known for.
stories.imageAlt: Crowds gather on Decatur Square for World Cup WatchFest

stories.headline: Messi Grabs Golden Boot Lead With His Eighth Goal in Atlanta
stories.summary: Lionel Messi scored again at Mercedes-Benz Stadium, pushing to the front of the World Cup's top-scorer race as the tournament rolls through its Atlanta matches.
stories.body: Atlanta keeps getting the Messi show. Lionel Messi scored his eighth goal of this World Cup during play at Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Downtown, moving into the lead for the Golden Boot, the award that goes to the tournament's top scorer. Atlanta landed a marquee slate of matches as one of the World Cup's American host cities, and the crowds downtown have made the most of it. Getting one of the greatest players of all time finding the net repeatedly in your building is about the best advertisement a host city could ask for. With the knockout rounds heating up, the Golden Boot race is one of the few individual storylines that can outshine the team drama. For now, Messi is out front, and a good chunk of his case was built right here.
stories.imageAlt: Lionel Messi celebrates a goal during the World Cup in Atlanta

stories.headline: Reynoldstown's Old Church Corner Becomes 'Gemini' Duplex Project
stories.summary: Two duplexes are rising at Gibson and Cummings streets, a block off the BeltLine's Southeast Trail, the latest intown infill to replace a former church.
stories.body: Another intown Atlanta church corner is becoming housing. In Reynoldstown, a project called Gemini is now fully underway at the northwest corner of Gibson and Cummings streets, according to Urbanize Atlanta. The plan calls for two separate duplexes from Alpharetta-based Kashi Custom Homes. The lot sits just a block east of the BeltLine's Southeast Trail, formerly known as the Eastside Trail, which puts it in one of the most in-demand pockets of intown real estate right now. Reynoldstown has been on this trajectory for a while. The neighborhood's stretch along the BeltLine has drawn steady infill and a major mixed-use redevelopment nearby, and small church-corner lots like this one keep getting redrawn as townhomes and duplexes. Whether that is a good trade depends on who you ask, but the pattern is unmistakable.
stories.imageAlt: Rendering of the Gemini duplex project on a former church corner in Reynoldstown

stories.headline: Atlanta History Center Opens Its Most Ambitious Exhibit for Its 100th Birthday
stories.summary: 'More Perfect Union: The American Civil War Era' fills roughly 9,000 square feet with hundreds of artifacts, marking a century since the center's founding.
stories.body: The Atlanta History Center in Buckhead is turning 100, and it is marking the occasion with the most ambitious exhibit it has ever attempted. "More Perfect Union: The American Civil War Era" opens July 10, spreading hundreds of artifacts across roughly 9,000 square feet. The center traces its own roots to October 1926, when the founding officers of the Atlanta Historical Society gathered downtown with no office space and stored donated artifacts wherever they could. A hundred years later, the institution is taking on one of the hardest subjects in American history and Atlanta's specific role in it. The framing is the interesting part. Rather than a tidy monument, the exhibit leans into the Civil War era as a contested record, which is a notably different posture than a lot of Southern institutions have historically taken. Expect a version of this story that argues with itself, which is probably the point.
stories.imageAlt: A regimental flag featured in the Atlanta History Center's More Perfect Union exhibit

stories.headline: Bellwood Coffee Says a New Jovita Moore Mural Is Finally in the Works
stories.summary: After backlash for painting over a tribute to the late WSB-TV anchor at its Grant Park cafe, the coffee company says a replacement mural is now being designed.
stories.body: A tribute to a beloved Atlanta news anchor is getting a second life after a rough start. Bellwood Coffee says a new mural honoring the late Jovita Moore is officially in the design process, according to Capital B Atlanta. The apology comes after real anger in Grant Park. Earlier this summer, residents discovered that Bellwood's new cafe had covered a colorful mural of Moore with dark gray paint and a business ad. Moore, the longtime WSB-TV anchor, died in 2021 at age 53 from brain cancer. The original piece, painted by local artist Tommy Bronx in November 2021, was commissioned by Atlanta United as part of a series honoring the city's figures. Painting over a memorial to a public figure that neighbors loved was never going to go quietly, and it did not. The company now says it is working on a replacement. The real test will be whether the new mural feels like a genuine tribute or a cleanup job.
stories.imageAlt: Bellwood Coffee cafe in Grant Park where a Jovita Moore mural was painted over

stories.headline: Barnes & Noble Returns to East Atlanta Four Years After Leaving
stories.summary: The bookseller reopened at the Edgewood Retail Center, drawing long morning lines from customers who never wanted it to go in the first place.
stories.body: The line formed early. When Barnes & Noble reopened at the Edgewood Retail Center on the morning of July 8, customers were waiting outside more than an hour before the doors opened. The shopping center on the east side of town, anchored by a Target and a Kroger, had a well-loved Barnes & Noble for years before the chain closed the location in 2022. Now it is back. Among the first in line were Lurelia Freeman and Sherry Young, Spelman College graduates from different generations who came out to welcome the store home. The quote that stuck, per The Atlanta Voice: "It didn't need to be taken out in the first place." A national chain reopening a store it closed a few years ago is not a common story, and the turnout says a lot about how much this particular bookstore meant to the neighborhood.
stories.imageAlt: Customers browse the new Barnes & Noble at the Edgewood Retail Center in East Atlanta

stories.headline: An Atlanta Startup Is Turning E-Trikes Into Rolling Digital Billboards
stories.summary: Purposers OOH is deploying battery-powered three-wheelers with digital ad screens along the BeltLine, Midtown, and the stadium district to catch this summer's crowds.
stories.body: This summer put an enormous, moving audience on Atlanta's streets, and one local startup wants to sell ads to it. Purposers OOH, founded by Midtown-area entrepreneurs James and Keisa Manning, is rolling out purpose-built e-trikes, three-wheeled battery-powered cycles, mounted with digital advertising screens. The pitch, per Hypepotamus, is targeting. Festival crowds, World Cup fans, and tourists are packing the BeltLine, Midtown, Buckhead, downtown, and the area around Mercedes-Benz Stadium. A static billboard cannot follow that foot traffic. An app-managed e-trike can roll to wherever the crowd is and swap what it shows on the fly. Call them mobile billboards if you want, and plenty of people will find another set of glowing screens on the BeltLine a little much. But as a bet on where Atlanta's attention physically is this summer, the idea is hard to argue with.
stories.imageAlt: A Purposers OOH e-trike carrying a digital advertising screen on an Atlanta street

stories.headline: G. Garvin's Midtown Steakhouse LowCountry Closes Without Warning
stories.summary: The upscale Southern steakhouse on West Peachtree, co-founded by the celebrity chef, shut down after its final dinner service with no reason given.
stories.body: One of Midtown's upscale dining rooms is gone with no heads-up. LowCountry Steak on West Peachtree Street has closed permanently, announcing the news on social media right after its final dinner service, per What Now Atlanta. The restaurant was a partnership between celebrity chef G. Garvin and restaurateur TC Mosby, serving a Southern-inspired steakhouse menu with dishes influenced by the Lowcountry region of the coastal Carolinas and Georgia. The closing announcement thanked customers for years of support but did not give a reason for shutting down. No-warning closures are always a little jarring, especially for a name-brand chef concept in the middle of Midtown. For now, all the owners have offered is a thank-you and a locked door.
stories.imageAlt: LowCountry Steak on West Peachtree Street in Midtown, now permanently closed

stories.headline: A Runner Dressed as a Hot Dog Became a Peachtree Road Race Legend
stories.summary: Mico Quijano ran the world's largest 10K in a hot dog costume, handing out foil-wrapped Costco dogs along the route, and now wants to make it a tradition.
stories.body: More than 56,000 people ran the Northside Hospital Peachtree Road Race on July 4, the world's largest 10K, along the hot and hilly 6.2 miles from Buckhead down to Midtown. Weaving through all of them was a giant hot dog. That was Mico Quijano, a runner and content creator from Charlotte running his first Peachtree dressed head to toe as a hot dog, pockets stuffed with ketchup packets and a tote bag full of foil-wrapped Costco dogs to hand out along the way, according to Rough Draft Atlanta. The Peachtree Road Race has always rewarded a good bit, and this one landed. Quijano says he wants to bring the hot dog back and make it an annual thing. In a race this big, becoming the person everyone remembers is its own kind of finish-line glory.
stories.imageAlt: A runner dressed as a hot dog during the Peachtree Road Race
